::: {.summary-section}
## Motivation and setup

Supersymmetry places a lower bound on the energy of a state with specified charges. States that saturate it are BPS states, the supersymmetric ground states in their charge sector. Black holes account for enormous numbers of such states, yet familiar regular BPS black holes do not exist at every allowed charge. This work asks what fills the rest of the phase diagram, and how these additional states affect the protected count called the superconformal index.

The setting is supergravity on $AdS_4\times S^7$, restricted to four electric charges equal in pairs. There are consequently two independent electric charges, $Q_1$ and $Q_2$, and one angular momentum, $J$. The BPS energy bound is

$$
E\ell\geq J+2(Q_{1}\ell+Q_{2}\ell)~.
$$

Here $\ell$ is the AdS radius. Saturating this linear inequality is necessary for supersymmetry, but a regular single black hole must also obey a nonlinear charge relation. After rescaling charges by the large-$N$ parameter $k=\ell^2/(2G)$, the paper uses densities $q_1,q_2,j$, their sum $q$, and difference $\tilde q$. The nonlinear relation defines the “black hole sheet”:

$$
\displaystyle j=j_{c}(q,\tilde{q})=q\left(\sqrt{1+4\left(q^{2}-\tilde{q}^{2}\right)}-1\right)~.
$$

This sheet is a surface in a three-dimensional charge space. It does not fill the physical region. Its geometry therefore exposes the central puzzle: generic supersymmetric charge sectors cannot be described by an isolated member of the known black-hole family. The paper proposes that they instead contain a black-hole core accompanied by another component carrying the remaining charge.

Light green is the translucent foreground; dark green shows the second branch where the sheet folds behind it. ([arXiv:2510.16274](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.16274))](../assets/papers/2510.16274/bhsheet.png){fig-alt="The curved green black-hole sheet in the three-dimensional space of charge densities."}

::: {.summary-section}
## Construction and results

The construction assumes a two-component system whose energy and charges add at leading order. One component is a BPS black hole; the other is termed a gas. The gas carries macroscopic charge but negligible leading entropy, so the total entropy comes from the core. In the large-$N$ thermodynamic description, these assumptions reduce the phase problem to a competition among possible core black holes. Grey-galaxy and dual-giant constructions motivate the two ways the additional component can carry charge.

Given total charges, the allowed cores lie on the black hole sheet and must leave nonnegative charges for the gas. The dominant candidate is found by maximizing the core entropy over that allowed set. On the sheet, the entropy density takes the simple form

$$
s_{BH}(j,q)=\pi\frac{j}{q}~.
$$

This constrained optimization produces distinct phases. On the overrotating side, called Region I, the entropy is greatest when the core retains all electric charge and the gas carries the excess angular momentum. This has the character of a grey galaxy, with angular momentum stored far from the central black hole.

On the overcharged side, Region II, the optimum places all angular momentum in the core while the gas carries electric charge. There are two cases. In Region IIa the core can reach equal electric charges, and the gas absorbs the charge imbalance. In Region IIb the positivity constraints prevent that equal-charge core; the optimum instead has gas carrying only one of the two electric charges. These charged configurations are motivated by dual giant gravitons, with an $M2$-brane interpretation in this compactification.

The superconformal index introduces another optimization. Because its chemical potentials obey a supersymmetric constraint, it resolves combinations of charges rather than all three charges independently. In the paper's density variables, an index line has fixed $\zeta=q+j$ and $\tilde\zeta=\tilde q$. Each physical line intersects the black hole sheet once, but this intersection need not supply its largest entropy.

Assuming that cancellations in the signed index do not remove the leading entropy maximum, the paper compares configurations along each line. For nonnegative $\tilde\zeta$, the resulting prediction is

$$
s_{\mathcal{I}}(\zeta,\tilde{\zeta})=\begin{cases}s_{X}(\zeta,\tilde{\zeta})&,~~{\rm if~~}\tilde{\zeta}\leq\frac{1}{2}\\
s_{max}(\zeta,\tilde{\zeta})&,~~{\rm if~~}\tilde{\zeta}>\frac{1}{2}\end{cases}
$$

The quantity $s_X$ is the entropy of the pure black hole at the intersection; $s_{max}$ is the larger two-component maximum. Exchanging the electric charges extends the transition to negative $\tilde\zeta$. Thus sufficiently unequal charges change the phase dominating the predicted index.
:::

::: {.summary-section}
## Phase transitions in the index

![Figure 2. The microcanonical index phase diagram in the physical region $|\tilde\zeta|\leq\zeta$. Grey is the pure BPS black-hole phase and blue is the two-component phase, connected by second-order transitions at $|\tilde\zeta|=1/2$. ([arXiv:2510.16274](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.16274))](../assets/papers/2510.16274/indphasediag.svg){fig-alt="The index phase diagram with a central grey black-hole region and blue two-component regions."}

The ground-state and index phase diagrams describe different ensembles. Fixing all conserved charges selects the best core compatible with one point in charge space. Fixing the index charges instead selects an entire line, along which angular momentum and the sum of electric charges vary together. The maximal entropy along this line determines the index prediction under the unobstructed saddle assumption. A two-component configuration can supply that maximum even though the line also contains a pure black hole.

When the electric charges are comparable, the entropy increases along the grey-galaxy segment toward the pure black hole and then decreases along the overcharged segment. The black-hole intersection is consequently the dominant point. For a sufficiently large charge difference, an additional maximum appears in the two-component part of the line. This maximum overtakes the pure black hole at $|\tilde\zeta|=1/2$, producing the second-order transition. At the positive boundary, the two entropy branches both equal $\pi(-1+\sqrt{2\zeta})$. Exchanging the two electric charges gives the corresponding negative boundary.

Complex Euclidean BPS black holes provide a complementary description through chemical potentials conjugate to the conserved charges. A convergent interpretation of the index requires the real parts of the relevant potentials to suppress towers of charged states. The onset of instability in this description coincides with the predicted transition to the two-component phase. The geometry and the statistical ensemble therefore identify the same threshold through different calculations.

The Kontsevich–Segal–Witten condition tests positivity of auxiliary-field kinetic terms on the complex metric. In this $AdS_4$ charge sector it remains satisfied across the statistical instability, distinguishing geometric allowability from thermodynamic dominance. Together, these results give a coherent organization of the leading large-$N$ ground states: entropy is stored in a black-hole core, charge can also reside in an accompanying component, and the index selects among these configurations according to the charge combinations it resolves.
:::
